topic.title: F = ma for a body in horizontal or vertical motion
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. F = ma in a straight line is never a question on its own: it sits inside a multi-part mechanics question, usually Q3 or Q6, where an earlier part draws the forces and a later one adds a constant-acceleration formula. Expect 5 to 8 marks of it, with the equation of motion carrying the method mark and the mass-for-weight slip costing the rest.
mustMemorise: F in F = ma is the resultant force along the line of motion
The m is the mass in kilograms; the weight mg in newtons goes on the diagram
Friction is given as a value or as a value per kilogram — multiply a per-kilogram rate by the mass
Choose a positive direction, write it down, and take the resultant in it
For a lift, up positive gives T - mg = ma
A 'show that' is derived forwards; verifying by substitution is capped at two marks
onFormulaSheet: v = u + at, v² = u² + 2as, s = ut + ½at², s = ½(u + v)t (Unit 2 formula sheet, page 2)
notOnThisSpec: F = μR and the coefficient of friction: the CCEA statement excludes them in terms, so friction is always a given value
Forces and motion in two dimensions, and components of a resultant acceleration
Momentum, impulse and collisions; Newton's third law as a named law with action-reaction pairs
Air resistance modelled as a function of speed, and terminal velocity
Stating modelling assumptions as an assessed answer

sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2, g = 10 m/s² on the front page. This never stands alone: it sits inside a multi-part mechanics question, usually Q3 or Q6. Summer 2025 Q6 ran friction, then the equation of motion, then further motion; Summer 2024 Q6 was a resistive force, a 'show that' for a mass, then the motion after a separation; Summer 2022 Q3(b) gave friction per kilogram and then changed the load. steps.working: For the box, taking the direction of motion as positive:
steps.decision: Name the body and the direction before any numbers. Examiners report forces on one body confused with forces on a whole system, and this line is what prevents it.

options: Because F = ma applies to one named body, and the forces must be that body's own
Because it is the conventional way to lay out the page
Because the direction of motion is always to the right
whyMenu.explain: A resultant only means something once you have said which body it acts on and which way you are calling positive. Both change the signs in the next line.

steps.decision: $F$ in $F = ma$ is the resultant along the line of motion, not one of the forces. Write the subtraction out so the resistance is visibly taken off.
The $m$ is the mass in kilograms. The $70$ N on the diagram is the weight, and it plays no part here because the box is not moving vertically.

steps.decision: The diagram needs the weight in newtons, so convert the mass once and write it on the arrow. This is the only place the two meet.

options: Because a force diagram is drawn in newtons, and a mass in kilograms is not a force
Because the mass must be converted before it can go into F = ma
Because weight and mass are two words for the same quantity
whyMenu.explain: The mass stays 500 kg and goes into $F = ma$ unchanged. It is only the downward arrow that needs newtons.

steps.decision: State the positive direction, then write the resultant in that direction. The cable pulls up and gravity pulls down, so the resultant is the difference.
The answer is positive, and up was positive, so the acceleration is upwards. Say so: a direction is part of the answer here.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a body has a mass of 6 kg. What is its weight, taking $g = 10$ m/s²?

options.feedback: Weight $= mg = 6 \times 10 = 60$ N.
That is the mass with a newton sign on it. Multiply by $g$ to turn a mass into a force.
That divides by $g$. Weight is the mass multiplied by $g$.
That is the mass again. A weight is a force, measured in newtons.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: rearrange $F = ma$ to make $a$ the subject.

options.feedback: $m$ is multiplying $a$, so divide both sides by $m$.
The fraction is upside down. Dividing both sides by $m$ leaves $F$ on top.
$ma$ is a product, so $m$ cannot be removed by subtracting it.
Multiplying by $m$ undoes nothing; it is division that clears it.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a rope costs 4 pounds per metre. What do 8 metres cost?

options.feedback: $4 \times 8 = 32$: a rate per unit is multiplied by the number of units.
That is the cost of one metre. Eight metres cost eight times as much.
That divides instead of multiplying.
That adds the two numbers. A rate per unit is multiplied.

items.skill: Mass or weight in F = ma
items.stem: A box of mass 5 kg, weight 50 N, is pushed by a resultant force of 30 N. What is its acceleration?

options.feedback: $30 = 5a$, so $a = 6$ m/s². The $m$ in $F = ma$ is the mass in kilograms.
That divides by the weight, 50 N. The weight belongs on the diagram, not in the equation.
That multiplies instead of dividing. $F = ma$ rearranges to $a = F \div m$.
That subtracts one number from the other. The relationship is a product, not a difference.

items.stem: A body is pushed by 60 N against a resistance of 20 N. Which number goes into $F = ma$?

options.feedback: $F$ is the resultant along the line of motion: $60 - 20 = 40$ N.
That is the driving force alone. The resistance is still acting, so it comes off first.
The resistance opposes the motion, so it is subtracted rather than added.
That is the resistance alone, which acts backwards.

items.stem: A resistance of 5 N per kg acts on a body of mass 9 kg. What is the resisting force?

options.feedback: $5 \times 9 = 45$ N: every kilogram is resisted by 5 N.
That is the force on one kilogram. Multiply by the mass to get the whole force.
That divides the mass by the rate. A rate per kilogram is multiplied by the mass.
That divides the other way round, and a force needs a unit.

items.stem: A lift of mass 300 kg hangs on a cable with tension 3300 N. Taking up as positive and $g = 10$ m/s², which equation is right?

options.feedback: The resultant upwards is the tension minus the weight, and the weight is $300 \times 10 = 3000$ N.
The weight is still acting. Leaving it out is the commonest slip on a vertical problem.
The weight acts downwards while the tension acts upwards, so they subtract.
That subtracts the mass rather than the weight. A force diagram is in newtons.

items.stem: A part says 'Show that the mass is 650 kg'. What earns the marks?

options.text: Forming the equation of motion and solving it for the mass
options.feedback: The forward route is what is being marked: build the equation from the diagram, then solve.

options.text: Putting 650 into the equation and showing both sides agree
options.feedback: That is verification, and CCEA caps it at two marks. It assumes what the part asks you to derive.

options.text: Writing down 650 kg with its units
options.feedback: The answer is already printed in the question, so writing it again shows nothing.

options.text: Drawing the force diagram on its own
options.feedback: The diagram is a good first step, but the equation and the solving are where the marks are.

parts.stem:
A lift of total mass 400 kg hangs on a vertical cable in which the tension is 4400 N.

Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: Turn the mass into a weight for the diagram.
Up positive: the resultant is the tension minus the weight.
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= 4000$ N. Taking up as positive, $4400 - 4000 = 400a$, so $a = 1$ m/s² upwards.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the tension alone by the mass, with the weight left out. Gravity is pulling down on the lift the whole time, so the resultant is the difference.
That writes the weight minus the tension, which is the resultant downwards. The size is right, so the method marks (M) stand; with up positive, the tension comes first.

context.setting: A service lift descending in a shaft

parts.stem:
A lift of total mass 400 kg hangs on a vertical cable in which the tension is 3600 N.

Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: The tension is smaller than the weight this time.
A negative answer with up positive means the acceleration is downwards; the magnitude is its size.
parts.workedSolution: Taking up as positive, $3600 - 4000 = 400a$ gives $a = -1$ m/s². The minus sign means the acceleration is 1 m/s² downwards, so its magnitude is 1 m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the tension divided by the mass, with the weight missing. The lift's weight is 4000 N and it never switches off.
With up positive the working does give $a = -1$, and the size is right, so the method marks (M) stand. The part asks for the magnitude: drop the sign and read it as 1 m/s² downwards.

context.setting: A wheeled bin pushed from rest along a yard

parts.stem:
A bin of mass 20 kg is pushed from rest along a rough horizontal yard by a horizontal force of 110 N against a resistance of 30 N.

Calculate how far it travels in the first 5 seconds.

Answer ________ m
hints: Find the acceleration first.

parts.workedSolution: For the bin: $110 - 30 = 20a$, so $a = 4$ m/s². From rest, $s = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 5^2 = 50$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: The $t$ in $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ has not been squared. Reaching the acceleration earns the method marks (M); square the time before multiplying.
That works from the driving force alone, with the resistance never taken off, so the acceleration used is too large.

parts.stem:
A crate of mass 8 kg is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 50 N. The resistance to motion is 3 N per kg of mass.

Calculate the total resistance to motion.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: Every kilogram of the crate is resisted by the same force.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the resistance on a single kilogram. The crate is 8 kg, so multiply.

parts.stem:
Calculate the acceleration of the crate.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: Resultant first, then $F = ma$ for the crate.
parts.workedSolution: For the crate: $50 - 24 = 8a$, so $26 = 8a$ and $a = 3.25$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That takes the 3 N per kilogram off as though it were the whole resistance. The resistance is 24 N, so the resultant is smaller than that.

parts.stem:
The crate starts from rest. Calculate its speed after 4 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: The acceleration is constant, so a constant-acceleration formula finishes it.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $\tfrac{1}{2}at$, which is neither a speed nor a distance. For a speed after a time, use $v = u + at$.

figures.alt: A lift of unknown mass M kilograms on a cable, with a tension of 7020 newtons upwards and its weight Mg downwards, accelerating upwards at 0.8 metres per second squared.

parts.stem:
A lift and its passengers have a total mass of $M$ kg. The lift hangs on a vertical cable in which the tension is 7020 N, and it accelerates upwards at 0.8 m/s².

Show that $M = 650$.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

[3]

accepted: Taking up as positive, 7020 - 10M = 0.8M, so 7020 = 10.8M and M = 650.

scheme.examinerNote: Verifying by substituting 650 into the equation is capped at two marks: the question asks for the forward derivation.

hints: Write the weight as $10M$ and the resultant as the tension minus it.
Collect the $M$ terms on one side.
parts.workedSolution: Taking up as positive, 7020 - 10M = 0.8M, so 7020 = 10.8M and M = 650.

commonErrors.feedback: Putting 650 into the equation and checking both sides agree is verification, not a derivation: CCEA caps that route at two of the three marks, and the forming and collecting lines it skips are the two marks being looked for here. Start from the forces and solve for $M$.
That leaves the weight out, so the tension alone is set equal to $Ma$. The lift's weight $10M$ is pulling down the whole time.

parts.stem:
The tension in the cable is now 6240 N.

Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of the lift.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: The mass is the one you just showed.
A negative answer with up positive means the acceleration points downwards.
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= 6500$ N. Taking up as positive, $6240 - 6500 = 650a$, so $a = -0.4$ m/s² and the acceleration is $0.4$ m/s² downwards.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the new tension by the mass with the weight left out. The weight is still 6500 N, and it is larger than the tension now, which is why the lift slows.
That divides the out-of-balance force by the weight rather than the mass. The forces are not balanced here, and $F = ma$ takes the mass in kilograms.
With up positive the working does give $a = -0.4$, and the size is right, so the method marks (M) stand. The part asks for the magnitude: drop the sign and read it as 0.4 m/s² downwards.

methodLock.requiredMethod: Form the equation of motion from the forces and solve it for M; substituting the printed value back in is verification and is capped at two marks.

findTheMistake.stem: Eoin is finding the acceleration of a 7 kg box pulled by 40 N against a resistance of 12 N, with $g = 10$ m/s². His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 4 puts the weight, 70 N, where $F = ma$ wants the mass. The weight is the right number for the downward arrow on the diagram, and line 3 works it out correctly, but it has no place in the equation of motion. Using it makes the acceleration ten times too small.
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the body and forming the resultant are both right, and they earn the two method marks (M). The habit that fixes the last line is to write the unit beside every number as you use it: kilograms go into the equation, newtons go on the diagram.

prompts.prompt: What does the $F$ in $F = ma$ stand for?
prompts.answer: The resultant force along the line of motion, not any single force acting.

prompts.prompt: Which of a body's two numbers goes into $F = ma$, the mass or the weight?
prompts.answer: The mass, in kilograms. The weight in newtons goes on the force diagram.

prompts.prompt: A resistance is given as 4 N per kg. How do you turn it into a force?
prompts.answer: Multiply it by the mass of the body, on its own line of working.

prompts.prompt: Why does CCEA never ask you for a coefficient of friction?
prompts.answer: Because $F = \mu R$ is excluded from this specification: friction is always given as a value, or as a value per unit mass.

prompts.prompt: What is the first line to write for a lift on a cable?
prompts.answer: The positive direction, then the resultant: the tension minus the weight equals the mass times the acceleration.

prompts.prompt: What does a 'show that' part want, and what does verifying cost?
prompts.answer: It wants the equation formed from the forces and solved forwards; substituting the printed answer back in is capped at two marks.

prompts.prompt: A later part increases the load. What has to change in the equation?
prompts.answer: The mass, because the body is heavier now; re-read the part and rebuild the equation before solving.
